title: Scaling up: The AI-Dependent Lawyer — LexisNexis UK Survey
author: LexisNexis · Artificial Lawyer · Nick Hilborne

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source shows frequent AI use in drafting, legal research and document review, with continuing accuracy concerns. This supports the cluster’s premise that AI is entering core legal workflows, but it does not assess whether this adoption is reducing junior production, leverage, revenue or apprenticeship opportunities, nor whether buyers are driving structural change.
qs: Moreover, 34% of the 500-plus lawyers surveyed said that they used AI tools for legal work every day, and 32% ‘multiple times per week’.
They also surfaced that the top three use cases are: drafting, legal research, and document review, which is to be expected.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The survey supports the cluster’s concern that direct public use can shift reliability and screening burdens downward: respondents widely perceive AI-driven legal misunderstanding, and a firm leader reports more potentially unmeritorious claims. However, this is perception-based evidence, not measured error rates or independently established litigation effects.
qs: Three-quarters (77%) of lawyers said AI was “causing clients or the general public to misinterpret the law”.
A leader at a large law firm reported a “huge increase in litigation, as claimants are able to harness AI to bring claims, not all of which will be meritorious”.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core account of AI as a rapidly adopted supporting tool for bounded legal tasks rather than demonstrated autonomous practice. Its survey evidence also reinforces concerns about fabricated information, confidentiality, overreliance and review burdens, although it does not directly establish productivity gains, apprenticeship effects or lawyer displacement.
qs: The most common use of AI was for legal research (69%), followed by document summarisation (62%) and drafting and document review (both 53%).
The proportion of people concerned about “inaccurate or fabricated AI-generated information” has also grown sharply, from 57% at the beginning of 2024 to 83%.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s augmentation-focused proposition by showing that AI is embedded in lawyers’ work, particularly drafting, research and document review, while reliability concerns persist. It adds adoption and anticipated recruitment effects, but does not establish AI-caused displacement or a particular staffing outcome.
qs: They also surfaced that the top three use cases are: drafting, legal research, and document review, which is to be expected.
Overall, all very promising for the field of legal AI – although some may of course be concerned that an increasing number of lawyers would not want to do their work without AI in a supporting role.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The survey supports the cluster’s core proposition that legal AI is being deployed mainly for bounded tasks within human-led workflows, while trust, authoritative sources, verification and organisational integration remain decisive. Its adoption and billing findings indicate substantial work redesign and market pressure, but do not establish general legal competence, autonomous replacement or realised organisation-wide value.

kp.k: Reported AI adoption reaches 94% of lawyers
kp.d: Legal Futures reports that LexisNexis gathered responses from 543 legal professionals for Scaling up: The AI-dependent lawyer. Reported use of AI for legal work reached 94%, compared with 61% last year, 41% the year before and 11% in 2023. These are survey adoption findings, rather than measures of productivity or work quality.
qs: Researchers at LexisNexis gathered responses from 543 legal professionals for the report Scaling up: The AI-dependent lawyer*.
LexisNexis’s survey found that 94% of lawyers now used AI for legal work, compared to 61% last year, 41% the year before and only 11% in 2023.

kp.k: Frequent usage varies across legal practice settings
kp.d: Legal Futures reports that three-quarters used AI at least weekly, 34% daily and 6% not at all. Weekly use was highest in in-house teams at 89%, compared with 68% in small law firms and just over half of barristers. Artificial Lawyer additionally reports 32% using AI multiple times per week.
qs: Moreover, 34% of the 500-plus lawyers surveyed said that they used AI tools for legal work every day, and 32% ‘multiple times per week’.
Three-quarters of lawyers used AI at least once a week, with 34% turning to it on a daily basis and only 6% saying they did not use the technology at all.
Adoption was particularly high in in-house legal teams, with 89% using AI at least once a week, compared to 68% of small law firms and just over half of barristers.

kp.k: Research, summarisation, drafting and review dominate reported uses
kp.d: Legal Futures identifies legal research as the most common use at 69%, followed by document summarisation at 62%, with drafting and document review both at 53%. Artificial Lawyer instead summarises the top three use cases as drafting, legal research and document review; the two accounts therefore present the task ordering differently.
qs: The most common use of AI was for legal research (69%), followed by document summarisation (62%) and drafting and document review (both 53%).
They also surfaced that the top three use cases are: drafting, legal research, and document review, which is to be expected.

kp.k: Self-reported dependence peaks in large firms
kp.d: One in 10 lawyers described themselves as dependent on AI to do their jobs, rising to 15% in large law firms and 13% in in-house teams. Artificial Lawyer interprets this dependence as evidence that AI has become a critical component of many lawyers’ work.
qs: One in 10 lawyers said they were “dependent” on AI to do their jobs. The proportion was highest in large law firms (15%) and in-house legal teams (13%).

It shows – especially on the usage and dependence points – that legal AI has become a critical part of many lawyers’ lives, in fact so much so that a notable number could not do their work without it.

kp.d: Concern about inaccurate or fabricated AI information increased from 57% at the beginning of 2024 to 83%. Other reported concerns were confidential data leakage (53%), excessive reliance (52%), declining work quality (27%), accidental bias (21%) and increased review workload (9%). These percentages measure respondents’ concerns, not observed error rates or demonstrated deterioration in legal work.
qs: The proportion of people concerned about “inaccurate or fabricated AI-generated information” has also grown sharply, from 57% at the beginning of 2024 to 83%.
After this, the most common concern was about confidential data leakage (53%) and becoming too reliant on AI (52%).
Just over a quarter (27%) worried that ‘my quality of work will decline’, with 21% concerned about accidental bias and 9% that ‘it will increase the volume of work I need to review’.

kp.k: Lawyers perceive public misunderstanding and AI-enabled litigation
kp.d: The survey reports that 77% believed AI was causing clients or the public to misinterpret law. Separately, an unnamed large-firm leader reported a substantial increase in litigation as claimants used AI to bring claims, some potentially unmeritorious. The latter is an attributed observation, not a quantified survey finding on litigation volumes.
qs: Three-quarters (77%) of lawyers said AI was “causing clients or the general public to misinterpret the law”.
A leader at a large law firm reported a “huge increase in litigation, as claimants are able to harness AI to bring claims, not all of which will be meritorious”.

kp.k: Legal grounding and oversight shape purchasing preferences
kp.d: Eight out of 10 lawyers felt more comfortable with AI grounded in legal sources, up from 70% a year earlier. Privacy and security, transparency about AI use and human oversight ranked ahead of cost, commercial value and output explainability as purchasing considerations. Artificial Lawyer links demand for verified sources to capabilities offered by major legal data providers.
qs: Eight out of 10 lawyers said they felt more comfortable using AI that was “grounded in legal sources”, a “noticeable increase” from 70% a year ago.
Lawyers’ main considerations when buying legal tech were strong data privacy and security standards, transparency about how AI was used, and “human oversight of AI-enabled services”.
These factors ranked ahead of cost and commercial value, or ability to explain outputs.

Understandably, the vast majority were still concerned about a potential risk for hallucinations and errors from AI tools, and equally understandably many favoured AI systems that could provide reassurance around accuracy and the use of verified sources – something that the major legal data providers can do.

kp.k: Organisational embedding lags widespread individual use
kp.d: Despite high reported adoption, fewer than a third said AI was embedded in their organisation’s strategy and operations, while 43% reported experimentation with slow progress. The source distinguishes widespread tool use from strategic and operational integration.
qs: Less than a third of legal professionals said AI was “already embedded in their organisation’s strategy and operations”, however, with 43% saying “they are experimenting but progress is slow”.

kp.k: More lawyers expect AI to change billing
kp.d: The share expecting AI to change how firms bill rose to 55% from 40% last year, particularly among large-firm lawyers and in-house teams. This is an expectation about future billing changes; the coverage does not identify a particular replacement pricing model or document realised changes.
qs: A majority of lawyers (55%) believed AI would change how firms billed, up from 40% last year. This was particularly true for large law firms and in-house legal teams.

kp.k: Report editor frames AI as supporting professional judgement
kp.d: LexisNexis report editor Dylan Brown interprets the findings as growing comfort with AI combined with greater demands for trust, accuracy and authority. His stated framing is augmentation of professional judgement rather than replacement.
qs: The findings point to a legal profession that is becoming more comfortable with AI, but more demanding about the trust, accuracy and authority behind it.
As adoption accelerates, lawyers increasingly want AI tools that support rather than replace professional judgement.

kp.k: Artificial Lawyer predicts talent shifts and vendor growth
kp.d: Artificial Lawyer predicts rising AI use and dependence, talent gravitating towards firms that support extensive AI usage, and expanding demand and customer retention for legal-AI vendors despite market-share competition. These are editorial extrapolations from the survey rather than measured recruitment or vendor-retention outcomes.
qs: Those numbers will only rise, meaning that legal talent will likely gravitate to those firms that support high levels of AI usage.
It also is manna from heaven* for the legal AI companies, i.e. their customers are not going anywhere – and there will be more of them.
There may be intense competition to control market share, but that market is only growing wider and deeper, it appears.

kp.k: Heavy usage raises unresolved token-cost allocation
kp.d: Artificial Lawyer identifies token costs as a consequence of heavy AI use, noting uncertainty about who ultimately pays. It qualifies this as potentially manageable and a sign of market maturation rather than necessarily a major obstacle.
qs: One side effect of heavy AI use is token costs.
This area is still in flux, but quite clearly someone, somewhere has to pay for the token usage.
Although, this is perhaps not a killer problem – and is a sign of a maturing market.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: AI use has become widespread and frequent among surveyed UK legal professionals, with a minority reporting dependence on it.
pts.d: Nick Hilborne reports LexisNexis survey findings that 94% now use AI for legal work, compared with 61% last year, 41% the preceding year and 11% in 2023. Three-quarters use it at least weekly and 34% daily. Artificial Lawyer additionally reports 32% using it multiple times per week. One in ten respondents describes dependence, rising to 15% in large firms and 13% in-house. Artificial Lawyer interprets these responses as evidence that AI has become critical to many lawyers' work, including an inference that some could not work without it.

pts.k: AI is being used for core legal tasks, although widespread individual use does not mean widespread organisational integration.
pts.d: Hilborne reports legal research as the most common use, at 69%, followed by document summarisation at 62%, and drafting and document review at 53% each. Artificial Lawyer separately characterises drafting, legal research and document review as the top three use cases. Hilborne reports that fewer than a third say AI is embedded in organisational strategy and operations, while 43% report slow experimentation.

pts.k: Increasing adoption accompanies growing concern about unreliable outputs and demand for trusted, supervised tools rather than replacement of professional judgement.
pts.d: Hilborne reports concern about errors and hallucinations rising from 57% at the beginning of 2024 to 83%; other concerns include confidential data leakage (53%), excessive reliance (52%), declining work quality (27%), accidental bias (21%) and increased review workload (9%). These are reported concerns, not measured outcomes. Eight in ten respondents feel more comfortable with AI grounded in legal sources, up from 70% a year earlier. Privacy, transparency and human oversight rank ahead of cost and commercial value or output explainability in purchasing considerations. Report editor Dylan Brown interprets the findings as demand for AI that supports rather than replaces professional judgement.

pts.k: Respondents believe AI contributes to public and client misunderstanding of law; one firm leader associates it with increased litigation, including potentially unmeritorious claims.
pts.d: Hilborne attributes the misunderstanding claim to 77% of surveyed lawyers. The litigation claim belongs specifically to an unnamed large-law-firm leader, who reports an increase because claimants can use AI to bring claims. Artificial Lawyer also reports the majority perception of misunderstanding and connects it to a separate Justice chatbot survey, without supplying that survey's findings in the document.

pts.k: A growing majority of respondents expects AI to change law-firm billing.
pts.d: Hilborne reports that 55% believe AI will change how firms bill, compared with 40% a year earlier, with the expectation particularly prominent among large firms and in-house teams. The document does not specify the future billing model, implementation date or actual billing changes.

pts.k: Artificial Lawyer predicts rising AI dependence, talent movement toward AI-supportive firms, and a growing, durable customer market for legal-AI vendors.
pts.d: The Artificial Lawyer commentary extrapolates from current use and dependence to predict further growth, likely attraction of legal talent to firms supporting high AI usage, and continued customer demand for legal-AI companies. It allows for intense competition over market share. These are the commentary's forecasts, not reported survey measurements of recruitment, retention or market growth.

pts.k: Artificial Lawyer identifies token costs as a consequence of heavy AI use, while suggesting they may not prevent market development.
pts.d: The commentary argues that increased usage entails token costs that someone must bear, without assigning those costs to a particular participant. It characterises pricing as unsettled and tentatively treats the issue as a sign of market maturity rather than a decisive obstacle. It also presents lawyers' expectations of AI support as potentially becoming normal, analogous to other workplace technology.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is a LexisNexis survey of 543 legal professionals; the document also includes respondent experience and editorial extrapolation.
pts.d: Both articles report the same UK LexisNexis research rather than independent surveys. Numerical adoption, dependence, concerns, purchasing preferences and billing expectations are respondent reports. Historical percentages are supplied, but fieldwork dates, sampling and weighting methods, subgroup sizes and comparability across survey waves are not described. The litigation assertion is one unnamed leader's experience. Brown's augmentation framing is an interpretation by the report editor. Artificial Lawyer's talent, customer-retention, market-growth and token-cost claims are commentary, with no separate recruitment, revenue, retention or cost data supplied. There are no model benchmarks or measured error rates in the text.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current findings are reported on 2 September 2026; comparisons look back to 2023–2025, while forward-looking claims have no fixed horizon.
pts.d: Both articles are dated 2 September 2026, but the survey's fieldwork period is unspecified. In that publication context, adoption comparisons refer to 2025, 2024 and 2023; error concerns compare with the beginning of 2024, and source-grounding preferences and billing expectations with a year earlier. Weekly and daily figures measure reported usage frequency. Artificial Lawyer forecasts further dependence and market growth without dates; talent movement is qualified as likely, competition as possible, and token costs as perhaps not a decisive problem. Brown's preference for augmentation is framed as accompanying accelerating adoption. Billing change is anticipated rather than established.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern UK legal practitioners, law-firm employers, corporate legal buyers, clients and the public, and legal-AI software providers.
pts.d: In-house teams show particularly frequent adoption: 89% report at least weekly use, compared with 68% in small firms and just over half of barristers. Large-firm lawyers have the highest reported dependence, followed by in-house lawyers. Practitioners use AI for research, summarisation, drafting and review, while expressing reliability, privacy and oversight concerns. Law firms face predicted effects on talent attraction and billing; in-house teams are especially likely to anticipate billing changes. Clients and the public are said to risk misunderstanding law, while claimants may use AI to initiate litigation. Legal-AI vendors are predicted to gain more durable and numerous customers, and Artificial Lawyer positions major legal-data providers as able to offer reassurance through verified sources. The document does not identify who ultimately bears token costs.
